newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court allows city billboard ad ban.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court allows city billboard ad ban.

text.p: The Supreme Court on Monday rejected a constitutional free-speech challenge to a Baltimore ban on billboards that advertise cigarettes or alcoholic beverages in many public places frequented by children.

The high court's action in the two cases occurred just three days after a federal judge in North Carolina ruled the U.S. Food and Drug Administration can regulate sales and labeling of cigarettes, but has no authority over advertising.

The Baltimore cases had been closely watched by the tobacco industry. The judge in North Carolina did not reach the constitutional free-speech question, ruling only on the more narrow issue that the FDA lacked the authority under the law to adopt the federal restrictions on advertising of cigarettes.
Baltimore adopted the two ordinances in 1994 in an effort to reduce illegal smoking and drinking by minors.

The laws were challenged in court by Anheuser-Busch Cos. Inc, the nation's largest brewer, and by Penn Advertising of Baltimore, which has a number of billboards in the city. They argued the laws violated their constitutional free-speech rights under the First Amendment.

But the Supreme Court rejected their appeals without any comment or dissent. The action does not create nationwide precedent, but leaves Baltimore's advertising restrictions in place and may encourage other cities to adopt similar measures.
